rationale: A wins because it separates the actual stories instead of slicing the same credit-risk loaf four ways. Its strongest move is “Brands get paid on day one. Who carries the 60-day float?” because that finds a real second protagonist B mostly misses. B has useful material, but “A wholesale marketplace becomes a bank: Faire's bet on embedded credit” is a dressed-up duplicate of its lender angle with a little category fog sprayed on it.
gaps_in_A: “rather than a bank score” is a small inference; the update says Faire uses order history, not that it rejects bank scores.
“cash flow, not demand” sharpens the retailer angle, but the update only says cash flow is the top barrier to ordering. Do not overclaim the contrast unless Faire has the survey table.
The set asks for valuation confirmation, but it should also ask for the date of the financing launch announcement if pitching after the 24-hour window.
gaps_in_B: “quietly becomes a lender” invents tone. Nothing in the update says this was quiet; that is newsroom perfume, not evidence.

“A wholesale marketplace becomes a bank” overstates the facts. Faire is underwriting 60-day inventory financing; calling it a bank is the kind of cute line that gets corrected by counsel before lunch.
“something only a marketplace at this scale ... could plausibly attempt” is invented category swagger. No comparison set was supplied, and the angle admits it needs comparison points.
The funding-mechanics, category-creation, and contrarian angles all orbit the same undisclosed-risk question. Meanwhile, B fails to carve out the brand-side story that A nails.
